newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesian rice imports from Burma seen down.
newsitem.headline: Indonesian rice imports from Burma seen down.

text.p: Indonesian imports of rice from Burma in the first nine months of this year are sharply down from 1995, a senior grains trader who visited Rangoon last week said on Wednesday.

"The data I obtained during the visit showed that between January and September this year, Indonesia had imported a mere 50,000 tonnes compared with 500,000 tonnes for the whole of 1995," he told Reuters.
He said Burma exported a total of 265,000 tonnes of rice in the first nine months of this year, compared with 655,000 tonnes for the whole of last year.
He said it was unclear if Indonesia might have ordered Burmese rice for shipments through the rest of the year, but added that Indonesia currently had ample rice stocks.
"They (Indonesia) may have ordered rice which has not been shipped yet. But the records show that in the first nine months of this year only 50,000 tonnes were shipped here," he said.

Indonesia's state logistics agency BULOG, which has a monopoly on rice imports, said late last month domestic rice stocks stood at 2.5 million tonnes at the end of October, down from 2.8 million tonnes in June.
BULOG chief Beddu Amang said Indonesia's unhusked rice production was projected to increase to 50 million tonnes this year from 49 million tonnes in 1995.

The U.S. embassy said in a report that Indonesia was expected to import 1.3 million tonnes of rice this year, compared with an estimated 3.25 million in 1995. It said 1997 imports were seen at 800,000 tonnes.
Indonesia took pride in being self-sufficient in rice until 1995 when a prolonged drought damaged crops.
The grains trader said Burma has also been trying to sell more corn to Indonesia, which bought 200 tonnes last year and has imported nothing up to September this year from Burma.
"They have been trying to sell corn to Indonesia but the pricing and poor quality posed problems," he said.
He expected Burma to export some 50,000 tonnes of corn this year based on export statistics obtained in Rangoon.
"Between January and September this year, Burma exported 30,500 tonnes, almost all to Malaysia," he said. "Corn exports only amounted to about 20,000 tonnes in 1995."

The trader said the sharp increase in corn exports in the first nine months of this year over 1995 could be due to an increase in production but added that there were no production data available in Rangoon.
He said domestic consumption in Burma was expected to increase as more feedmills are built.
"Many companies are beginning to set up operations in Burma and once the political situation there is sorted out, I see a tremendous potential in trade there," he added.
